newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pasqua weighs in with attack on French EMU policy.
newsitem.headline: Pasqua weighs in with attack on French EMU policy.

text.p: Senior parliamentarian and anti-Maastricht campaigner Charles Pasqua threw his weight behind other critics of the French government's policy on European monetary union on Thursday.

Pasqua issued a statement welcoming remarks by former President Valery Giscard d'Estaing, who on Wednesday questioned France's "strong franc" policy and called for depreciation of the franc to favour economic growth and employment on the way to EMU.

"Mr Giscard d'Estaing's analysis meets mine and above all that of the French people, who are questioning in increasing number a policy devoted solely to the creation of the euro in unfavourable conditions for the economy, investment and jobs," said Pasqua.

Earlier Philippe Seguin, Gaullist National Assembly Speaker and another anti-Maastricht campaigner, said the former president's remarks were "impeccable," "good sense" and had put the debate on Europe back on the right footing with employment as absolute priority.

"I have long campaigned for a policy which would found the European currency on growth and employment rather than coming before it. It's about involving people in the heart of the process," Pasqua said.
"I am delighted to see these ideas gaining ground. This debate is indeed a debate about the future of France. And now it is also a debate about the future of Europe," he said.

On Thursday, Giscard d'Estaing, who has long been associated with the construction of Europe, appeared to modify somewhat the comments he first made in L'Express magazine, at least as far as the rate of the franc versus the mark was concerned.

After meeting German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Bonn, Giscard d'Estaing told reporters: "The link between the franc and the mark is no problem." He said the problem was the level of the franc versus the dollar and that he would prefer to see the U.S. currency at 5.5 francs rather than closer to 5.0 at the moment.
